title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 46 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 355–360 (Night 46, continuing directly from nights-45), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 46 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The envoys of the king of Constantinople present their gift; the old vizier Dandān advises sending an army, and ʿUmar sends his son Sharkān with ten thousand horsemen, with Dandān beside him. After twenty days' march they camp in a wide valley on the edge of the Byzantine lands, where Sharkān, riding out alone, falls asleep in the saddle, wakes in a forest, and overhears a band of girls wrestling by a river near a monastery; the night ends as the fair girl accepts the old woman's challenge to wrestle. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-arbaʿūn
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth and the forty,
sentences.i: And when it was the forty-sixth night,
sentences.n: This is the formula that opens each night. The ordinal is built the Arabic way, units before tens: "the sixth and the forty". كَانَتْ is used in its full sense, "there came / it arrived", so اللَّيْلَةُ is its subject; the final كَانَتِ carries a kasra only to bridge into the article that follows.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْعَسْكَرَ وَالرُّسُلَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ عِنْدِ مَلِكِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ لَمَّا قَبَّلُوا الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ بَعْدَ أَنْ حَكَوْا لَهُ وَأَخْرَجُوا لَهُ الْهَدِيَّةَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ʿaskara wa-al-rusula alladhīna min ʿindi maliki al-Qusṭanṭīniyyati lammā qabbalū al-arḍa bayna yadayi al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni baʿda an ḥakaw lahu wa-akhrajū lahu al-hadiyya
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king, the happy, that the army and the messengers who are from the presence of the king of Constantinople, when they kissed the ground between the two hands of King ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān, after they had related to him and brought out to him the gift —
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the host and the envoys from the king of Constantinople had kissed the ground before King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and had delivered their message to him and brought forth the gift —
sentences.n: The sentence is left hanging: this that-clause (أَنَّ …) is not completed until the king's reaction two units on, resumed by فَلَمَّا رَآهُمُ. The edition prints السعيدان as a single word, al-saʿīd + anna with no space between them; it is kept run together exactly as printed and pointed as two words fused. In العسكر والرسل the "army" is the escort and the "messengers" the envoys who brought the gift.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتِ الْهَدِيَّةُ خَمْسِينَ جَارِيَةً مِنْ خَوَاصِّ بِلَادِ الرُّومِ وَخَمْسِينَ مَمْلُوكًا عَلَيْهِمْ أَقْبِيَةٌ مِنَ الدِّيبَاجِ بِمَنَاطِقَ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَكُلُّ مَمْلُوكٍ فِي أُذُنِهِ حَلْقَةٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ فِيهَا لُؤْلُؤَةٌ تُسَاوِي أَلْفَ مِثْقَالٍ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْجَوَارِي كَذَلِكَ وَعَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ الْقُمَاشِ مَا يُسَاوِي مَالًا جَزِيلًا
sentences.tr: wa-kānati al-hadiyyatu khamsīna jāriyatan min khawāṣṣi bilādi al-Rūmi wa-khamsīna mamlūkan ʿalayhim aqbiyatun mina al-dībāji bi-manāṭiqa mina al-dhahabi wa-al-fiḍḍati wa-kullu mamlūkin fī udhunihi ḥalqatun mina al-dhahabi fīhā luʾluʾatun tusāwī alfa mithqālin mina al-dhahabi wa-al-jawārī kadhālika wa-ʿalayhim mina al-qumāshi mā yusāwī mālan jazīl
sentences.l: And the gift was fifty slave-girls of the choice-ones of the lands of Rūm, and fifty mamlūks, upon them coats of brocade with girdles of gold and silver, and every mamlūk in his ear a ring of gold, in it a pearl worth a thousand mithqāls of gold; and the slave-girls likewise, and upon them of cloth what is worth wealth abundant.
sentences.i: The gift was fifty slave-girls from the choicest of the lands of Rūm and fifty mamlūks, clad in brocade coats with girdles of gold and silver, each mamlūk with a gold ring in his ear set with a pearl worth a thousand mithqāls of gold; the girls were the same, and the clothing they wore was worth a vast sum.
sentences.n: الرُّوم are the Byzantine Greeks, the lands of the eastern Roman empire. A مِثْقَال is a weight, in practice that of a dinar (a little over four grams), so the pearl is priced in weight of gold. The masculine plural in وَعَلَيْهِمْ is used of the slave-girls too ("and upon them"), a Middle Arabic habit of letting the masculine plural stand for a mixed or female group. بِمَنَاطِقَ is the diptote plural of مِنْطَقَة, a girdle or belt.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُمُ الْمَلِكُ قَبِلَهُمْ وَفَرِحَ بِهِمْ وَأَمَرَ بِإِكْرَامِ الرُّسُلِ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَى وُزَرَائِهِ وَاسْتَشَارَهُمْ فِيمَا يَفْعَلُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhumu al-maliku qabilahum wa-fariḥa bihim wa-amara bi-ikrāmi al-rusuli wa-aqbala ʿalā wuzarāʾihi wa-istashārahum fīmā yafʿal
sentences.l: And when the king saw them, he accepted them and rejoiced in them, and he ordered the honouring of the messengers, and turned upon his viziers and consulted them about what he should do.
sentences.i: When the king saw them he accepted them and rejoiced in them; he commanded that the envoys be honoured, and turned to his viziers and took counsel with them as to what he should do.
sentences.n: The edition prints قبلهم, which the letters allow to be either qabilahum, "accepted them", or qabbalahum, "kissed them". We read the former: the king receives the human gifts, and a king does not kiss slaves. This is a reading, not a certainty. أَمَرَ بِـ is the verb's own preposition, "order (the doing of)"; أَقْبَلَ عَلَى is "turn to, address".

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَ مِنْ بَيْنِهِمْ وَزِيرٌ وَكَانَ شَيْخًا كَبِيرًا يُقَالُ لَهُ دَنْدَانُ فَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَقَالَ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ مَافِى الْأَمْرِ أَحْسَنُ إِلَّا أَنْ تُجَهِّزَ عَسْكَرًا جَرَّارًا وَتُقَدِّمَ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَدَكَ شَرْكَانَ وَنَحْنُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ غِلْمَانٌ
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍa min baynihim wazīrun wa-kāna shaykhan kabīran yuqālu lahu Dandānu fa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayi al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni wa-qāla ayyuhā al-maliku māfī al-amri aḥsanu illā an tujahhiza ʿaskaran jarrāran wa-tuqaddima ʿalayhim waladaka Sharkāna wa-naḥnu bayna yadayhi ghilmān
sentences.l: So there rose from among them a vizier — and he was an old man, great, it was said to him Dandān — and he kissed the ground between the two hands of King ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān and said: O king, nothing in the matter is better than that you equip an army, dragging, and set over them your son Sharkān, and we before his two hands, lads.
sentences.i: Then a vizier rose from among them, a great old man called Dandān, and he kissed the ground before King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān and said: O king, nothing could be better than that you equip a mighty host and set your son Sharkān over it, while we attend him as his lads.
sentences.n: The edition prints فى for في and runs it into the word before it, مافى; both are kept. مَا … أَحْسَنُ إِلَّا is "nothing is better except", the negative-plus-except frame for "the best course is". جَرَّار, literally "dragging", is the dictionary word for an army so numerous that it trails along behind itself. غِلْمَان, "lads", is the vizier's modest word for himself and his colleagues as Sharkān's attendants.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا الرَّأْيُ عِنْدِي أَحْسَنُ لِوَجْهَيْنِ الْأَوَّلُ أَنَّ مَلِكَ الرُّومِ قَدِ اسْتَجَا رَبِكَ وَأَرْسَلَ إِلَيْكَ هَدِيَّةً فَقَبِلْتَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā al-raʾyu ʿindī aḥsanu li-wajhayni al-awwalu anna malika al-Rūmi qadi istajāra bika wa-arsala ilayka hadiyyatan fa-qabiltahā
sentences.l: And this opinion with me is better for two aspects: the first, that the king of Rūm has sought-protection of you and sent to you a gift, and you accepted it.
sentences.i: And this counsel seems to me the better for two reasons. The first is that the king of Rūm has sought your protection and sent you a gift, which you have accepted.
sentences.n: The edition prints استجا ربك, two words divided in the wrong place: it is a misdivision of اِسْتَجَارَ بِكَ, "he sought your protection". We keep the printed division and point each piece so that the letters stand unchanged; read them together as istajāra bika. Do not take رَبِكَ for "your Lord" (rabbuka): the vowels given here make it the tail of the verb plus the preposition. لِوَجْهَيْنِ is literally "for two faces", that is, two aspects or grounds.

sentences.t: وَالْوَجْهُ الثَّانِي أَنَّ الْعَدُوَّ لَايَجْسُرُ فَإِذَا مَنَعَ عَسْكَرُكَ عَنْ مَلِكِ الرُّومِ وَانْكَسَرَ عَدُوُّهُ يُنْسَبُ هَذَا الْأَمْرُ إِلَيْكَ وَيَشِيعُ ذَلِكَ فِي سَائِرِ الْأَقْطَارِ وَالْبِلَادِ وَلَاسِيَّمَا إِذَا وَصَلَ الْخَبَرُ إِلَى جَزَائِرِ الْبَحْرِ وَيَسْمَعُ ذَلِكَ أَهْلُ الْمَغْرِبِ فَيَحْمِلُونَ إِلَيْكَ الْهَدَايَا وَالتُّحَفَ وَالْأَمْوَالَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-wajhu al-thānī anna al-ʿaduwwa lāyajsuru fa-idhā manaʿa ʿaskaruka ʿan maliki al-Rūmi wa-inkasara ʿaduwwuhu yunsabu hādhā al-amru ilayka wa-yashīʿu dhālika fī sāʾiri al-aqṭāri wa-al-bilādi wa-lāsiyyamā idhā waṣala al-khabaru ilā jazāʾiri al-baḥri wa-yasmaʿu dhālika ahlu al-maghribi fa-yaḥmilūna ilayka al-hadāyā wa-al-tuḥafa wa-al-amwāl
sentences.l: And the second aspect: that the enemy does not dare; so when your army wards off from the king of Rūm and his enemy is broken, this matter is ascribed to you, and that spreads in all the regions and the lands, and especially when the news reaches the islands of the sea and the people of the West hear that, so they bring to you the gifts and the rarities and the monies.
sentences.i: The second reason is that the enemy dares not [face them]; so when your army has defended the king of Rūm and his foe lies broken, the deed will be put to your credit and the tale of it will run through every region and land — above all when the news reaches the islands of the sea and the people of the West hear it and send you gifts, rarities and treasure.
sentences.n: لَايَجْسُرُ is printed as one word (lā + yajsuru) and has no complement: Classical would say "does not dare to …". We keep the bare verb; the edition may have dropped words, and the bracket in the idiomatic line only marks the gap. مَنَعَ عَنْ is "to defend, ward off from"; the passive مُنِعَ would fit the letters too, but the active reading gives عَسْكَرُكَ a verb of its own. The conclusion يُنْسَبُ comes with no فَ before it, which is common after an إِذَا clause. وَلَاسِيَّمَا is "and especially".

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ هَذَا أَعْجَبَهُ كَلَامُ وَزِيرِهِ وَاسْتَصْوَبَهُ وَخَلَعَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ مِثْلُكَ مَنْ تَسْتَشِيرُهُ الْمُلُوكُ وَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ تَكُونَ أَنْتَ فِي مُقَدَّمِ الْعَسْكَرِ وَوَلَدِي شَرْكَانُ فِي سَاقَةِ الْعَسْكَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku hādhā aʿjabahu kalāmu wazīrihi wa-istaṣwabahu wa-khalaʿa ʿalayhi wa-qāla lahu mithluka man tastashīruhu al-mulūku wa-yanbaghī an takūna anta fī muqaddami al-ʿaskari wa-waladī Sharkānu fī sāqati al-ʿaskar
sentences.l: And when the king heard this, the speech of his vizier pleased him, and he deemed it right, and cast a robe upon him; and he said to him: One like you is he whom the kings consult; and it is fitting that you be in the front of the army, and my son Sharkān in the rear of the army.
sentences.i: When the king heard this, his vizier's words pleased him and he judged them sound; he bestowed a robe of honour on him and said: A man like you is one whom kings consult. It is right that you take the van of the army, with my son Sharkān in its rear.
sentences.n: خَلَعَ عَلَيْهِ, "he cast (a robe) upon him", is the standard idiom for bestowing a robe of honour. The king does not simply accept Dandān's plan: where the vizier proposed Sharkān at the head of the army, the king puts Dandān in the van and Sharkān in the rear. The last clause, وَوَلَدِي شَرْكَانُ فِي سَاقَةِ الْعَسْكَرِ, has no verb of its own; it is read as "and my son Sharkān (being) in the rear", continuing the king's proposal.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ أَمَرَ بِإِحْضَارِ وَلَدِهِ شَرْكَانَ فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ قَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ وَالِدِهِ وَجَلَسَ فَقَصَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقِصَّةَ وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِمَا قَالَهُ الرُّسُلُ وَبِمَا قَالَهُ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ وَأَوْصَاهُ بِأَخْذِ الْأُهْبَةِ وَالتَّجْهِيزِ لِلسَّفَرِ وَأَنَّهُ لَا يُخَالِفُ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ فِيمَا يَفْعَلُ وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يَنْتَخِبَ مِنْ عَسْكَرِهِ عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ كَامِلِينَ الْعُدَّةَ صَابِرِينَ عَلَى الْحُرُوبِ وَالشِّدَّةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika amara bi-iḥḍāri waladihi Sharkāna fa-lammā ḥaḍara qabbala al-arḍa bayna yaday wālidihi wa-jalasa fa-qaṣṣa ʿalayhi al-qiṣṣata wa-akhbarahu bi-mā qālahu al-rusulu wa-bi-mā qālahu al-wazīru Dandānu wa-awṣāhu bi-akhdhi al-uhbati wa-al-tajhīzi li-al-safari wa-annahu lā yukhālifu al-wazīra Dandāna fīmā yafʿalu wa-amarahu an yantakhiba min ʿaskarihi ʿasharata ālāfi fārisin kāmilīna al-ʿuddata ṣābirīna ʿalā al-ḥurūbi wa-al-shidda
sentences.l: Then indeed the king ordered the bringing-present of his son Sharkān; and when he was present, he kissed the ground between the two hands of his father and sat; and he related to him the story and informed him of what the messengers said and of what the vizier Dandān said, and charged him with the taking of the equipment and the preparation for the journey, and that he not oppose the vizier Dandān in what he does; and he ordered him that he select from his army ten thousand horsemen, complete-ones as to equipment, enduring-ones in the wars and the hardship.
sentences.i: Then the king sent for his son Sharkān, and when he came he kissed the ground before his father and sat down. The king told him the whole affair, what the envoys had said and what the vizier Dandān had said, and charged him to take up his gear and make ready for the journey, and that he must never go against the vizier Dandān in whatever he did. And he commanded him to pick out of his army ten thousand horsemen, fully equipped and steadfast in war and hardship.
sentences.n: أَوْصَى بِـ is "to charge someone with (a task)"; الْأُهْبَة is equipment and readiness for an undertaking. وَأَنَّهُ … is the second of the things he is charged with, "and that he not oppose the vizier Dandān": Sharkān is not to overrule him. كَامِلِينَ الْعُدَّةَ keeps the plural nūn and takes the equipment in the accusative ("complete as to equipment"), the loose Middle Arabic way of what Classical would write كاملي العدة.

sentences.t: فَامْتَثَلَ شَرْكَانُ لِمَا قَالَ لَهُ أَبُوهُ عُمَرُ بْنُ النُّعْمَانِ وَقَامَ فِى الْوَقْتِ وَاخْتَارَ مِنْ عَسْكَرِهِ عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ ثُمَّ دَخَلَ قَصْرَهُ وَعَرَضَ عَسْكَرَهُ وَأَنْفَقَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْمَالَ وَقَالَ لَهُمُ الْمُهْلَةُ عَلَيْكُمْ ثَلَٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-imtathala Sharkānu li-mā qāla lahu abūhu ʿUmaru ibnu al-Nuʿmāni wa-qāma fī al-waqti wa-ikhtāra min ʿaskarihi ʿasharata ālāfi fārisin thumma dakhala qaṣrahu wa-ʿaraḍa ʿaskarahu wa-anfaqa ʿalayhimu al-māla wa-qāla lahumu al-muhlatu ʿalaykum thalāthata ayyām
sentences.l: So Sharkān complied with what his father ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān had said to him, and rose at the time, and chose from his army ten thousand horsemen; then he entered his palace, and mustered his army, and spent upon them the money, and said to them: The respite upon you (is) three days.
sentences.i: So Sharkān did as his father ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān had told him, and rose that very hour and chose ten thousand horsemen from his army. Then he went into his palace, reviewed his troops, paid out money to them, and said: You have three days' grace.
sentences.n: The edition prints ثلثة for ثلاثة, with no alif for the long ā. It is pointed here with a dagger alif (ثَلَٰثَةَ), so the printed letters stay as they are and the word reads thalātha. فِى is the edition's spelling for في. لِمَا قَالَ لَهُ: امتثل takes لِـ for the thing obeyed. الْمُهْلَةُ عَلَيْكُمْ ثَلَٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ is a verbless sentence, "the respite is upon you, three days", with the three days as accusative of duration.

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلُوا الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مُطِيعِينَ لِأَمْرِهِ وَخَرَجُوا مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَأَخَذُوا فِى الْأُهْبَةِ وَإِصْلَاحِ الشَّأْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbalū al-arḍa bayna yadayhi muṭīʿīna li-amrihi wa-kharajū min ʿindihi wa-akhadhū fī al-uhbati wa-iṣlāḥi al-shaʾn
sentences.l: So they kissed the ground between his two hands, obedient-ones to his command, and went out from his presence, and took to the preparation and the setting-right of the matter.
sentences.i: They kissed the ground before him, obedient to his command, and left his presence and set about their preparations and putting all in order.
sentences.n: قَبَّلُوا الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ, "they kissed the ground between his hands", is the courtly gesture of homage; you will meet it again in the next units. أَخَذُوا فِى is "began, set about", a common Arabic use of أخذ with a following noun.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَرْكَانَ دَخَلَ إِلَى خَزَائِنِ السِّلَاحِ وَأَخَذَ جَمِيعَ مَايَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ مِنَ الْعُدَدِ وَالسِّلَاحِ ثُمَّ دَخَلَ الْإِصْطَبْلَ وَاخْتَارَ مِنْهُ الْخَيْلَ الْمُسَوَّمَةَ وَغَيْرَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Sharkāna dakhala ilā khazāʾini al-silāḥi wa-akhadha jamīʿa māyaḥtāju ilayhi mina al-ʿudadi wa-al-silāḥi thumma dakhala al-iṣṭabla wa-ikhtāra minhu al-khayla al-musawwamata wa-ghayrahum
sentences.l: Then indeed Sharkān entered the storehouses of the weaponry, and took all that he needed of the gear and the weaponry; then he entered the stable, and chose from it the marked horses and others than them.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān went into the armouries and took all the gear and weapons he needed. Then he entered the stable and chose from it the finest horses, and others besides.
sentences.n: The edition prints مايحتاج as one word, ما يحتاج, "what he needs"; it is vocalised in place as مَايَحْتَاجُ, so the printed letters stay in one piece. الْمُسَوَّمَة is the Qurʾānic epithet of fine horses (3:14); the lexicons give both "marked/branded" and "put out to pasture", and the English "finest horses" is a hedge between them. وَغَيْرَهُمْ is masculine plural, "others", the pronoun going back to the horses as individuals.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ أَقَامُوا ثَلَٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ ثُمَّ خَرَجَتِ الْعَسَاكِرُ إِلَى ظَاهِرِ مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika aqāmū thalāthata ayyāmin thumma kharajati al-ʿasākiru ilā ẓāhiri madīnati Baghdād
sentences.l: And after that they stayed three days; then the armies went out to the outside of the city of Baghdād.
sentences.i: After that they stayed three days; then the troops marched out to the outskirts of Baghdad.
sentences.n: ظَاهِر الْمَدِينَة is "the outside of the city": the troops encamp beyond the walls. خَرَجَتِ العساكر puts the verb in the feminine singular, the normal agreement for a plural of things.

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَ عُمَرُ بْنُ النُّعْمَانِ لِوَدَاعِ وَلَدِهِ شَرْكَانَ فَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَأَهْدَى لَهُ سَبْعَ خَزَائِنَ مِنَ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-kharaja ʿUmaru ibnu al-Nuʿmāni li-wadāʿi waladihi Sharkāna fa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi wa-ahdā lahu sabʿa khazāʾina mina al-māl
sentences.l: And ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān went out for the farewell-of his son Sharkān; so he kissed the ground between his two hands, and he presented to him seven treasuries of the money.
sentences.i: ʿUmar son of al-Nuʿmān came out to bid his son Sharkān farewell, and Sharkān kissed the ground before him, and the king gave him seven treasuries' worth of money.
sentences.n: The subject changes twice inside the sentence: ʿUmar comes out; Sharkān kisses the ground; ʿUmar gives the gift. The Arabic does not signal this, and a reader must follow the sense. خزائن (here "treasuries", "chests") is the same word as in the armouries two units earlier; the gift is seven stores' worth of money, probably in sealed purses.

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَى الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ وَأَوْصَاهُ بِعَسْكَرِ وَلَدِهِ شَرْكَانَ فَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَأَجَابَهُ بِالسَّمْعِ وَالطَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-aqbala ʿalā al-wazīri Dandāna wa-awṣāhu bi-ʿaskari waladihi Sharkāna fa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi wa-ajābahu bi-al-samʿi wa-al-ṭāʿa
sentences.l: And he turned to the vizier Dandān, and charged him with the army of his son Sharkān; so he kissed the ground between his two hands, and answered him with hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: Then the king turned to the vizier Dandān and charged him with the care of his son Sharkān's army, and the vizier kissed the ground before him and answered with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: The subjects shift again: the king turns to the vizier; the vizier kisses the ground and answers. بِالسَّمْعِ وَالطَّاعَةِ, "with hearing and obedience", is the standard formula of acceptance. أَوْصَى بِـ is "to commend, to charge with the care of".

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلَ الْمَلِكُ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ شَرْكَانَ وَأَوْصَاهُ أَنَّهُ يُشَاوِرُ الْوَزِيرَ فِي جَمِيعِ أُمُورِهِ فَقَبِلَ ذَٰلِكَ وَرَجَعَ وَالِدُهُ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-aqbala al-maliku ʿalā waladihi Sharkāna wa-awṣāhu annahu yushāwiru al-wazīra fī jamīʿi umūrihi fa-qabila dhālika wa-rajaʿa wāliduhu ilā an dakhala al-madīna
sentences.l: And the king turned to his son Sharkān, and charged him that he consults the vizier in all of his affairs; so he accepted that, and his father went back until he entered the city.
sentences.i: The king turned again to his son Sharkān and charged him to take counsel with the vizier in all his affairs; Sharkān agreed, and his father went back till he had entered the city.
sentences.n: أَنَّهُ يُشَاوِرُ puts the indicative after أَنَّ, where Classical Arabic would have أَنْ يُشَاوِرَ after أَوْصَى: a Middle Arabic habit, vocalised as printed. وَرَجَعَ وَالِدُهُ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ puts the verb before its subject, and إِلَى أَنْ + perfect means "until". The "father" here is ʿUmar, who goes back into Baghdad.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَرْكَانَ أَمَرَ النُّقَبَاءَ بِالْعَرْضِ فَعَرَضُوا الْعَسَاكِرَ وَكَانَتْ عِدَّتُهُمْ عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ فَارِسٍ غَيْرَ مَا يَتْبَعُهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Sharkāna amara al-nuqabāʾa bi-al-ʿarḍi fa-ʿaraḍū al-ʿasākira wa-kānat ʿiddatuhum ʿasharata ālāfi fārisin ghayra mā yatbaʿuhum
sentences.l: Then indeed Sharkān ordered the captains to the review, so they reviewed the armies; and their number was ten thousand horsemen, other-than what follows them.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān ordered the captains to hold a muster, and they mustered the troops, whose number was ten thousand horsemen, besides those who followed in their train.
sentences.n: النُّقَبَاء are the captains (nuqabāʾ, sing. naqīb), the officers who count and muster the companies. عِدَّتُهُمْ means "their number"; the word also means "equipment", and the text used it in that other sense a few units back (الْعُدَّة), so the repetition is a small play. غَيْرَ مَا يَتْبَعُهُمْ, "apart from what follows them", covers camp-followers and baggage-men, who are not counted among the ten thousand.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْقَوْمَ حَمَلُوا وَدُقَّتِ الطُّبُولُ وَزَعَقَتِ الْبُوقَاتُ وَانْتَشَرَتِ الْأَعْلَامُ وَالرَّايَاتُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-qawma ḥamalū wa-duqqati al-ṭubūlu wa-zaʿaqati al-būqātu wa-intasharati al-aʿlāmu wa-al-rāyāt
sentences.l: Then indeed the folk charged / moved-off, and the drums were beaten, and the trumpets blared, and the standards and the banners spread-out.
sentences.i: Then the host moved off: the drums were beaten, the trumpets blared, and the standards and banners were unfurled.
sentences.n: حَمَلُوا is uncertain. Lane gives حمل عليه "he charged him"; used alone of an army it can mean "set off, advanced", and a second sense, "loaded up" (the baggage), is also possible. The following list of drums, trumpets and banners tells you a march is starting, so "moved off" is the safest reading. Note that دُقَّتْ is passive ("were beaten") while زَعَقَتْ is active ("blared"); the edition prints the plain letters and the pointing is ours.

sentences.t: وَرَكِبَ ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانُ وَإِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَزِيرُهُ دَنْدَانُ وَالْأَعْلَامُ تَخْفِقُ عَلَى رُؤُسِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-rakiba ibnu al-maliki Sharkānu wa-ilā jānibihi wazīruhu Dandānu wa-al-aʿlāmu takhfiqu ʿalā ruʾusihim
sentences.l: And the son-of the king, Sharkān, rode, and at his side his vizier Dandān, and the standards fluttering over their heads.
sentences.i: Prince Sharkān rode, with his vizier Dandān at his side and the standards fluttering above their heads.
sentences.n: ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانُ: "the king's son, Sharkān", with ibn in the nominative and the name in apposition. وَالْأَعْلَامُ تَخْفِقُ is a circumstantial clause ("with the standards fluttering"), introduced by wa-. The edition spells the plural "heads" رؤسهم, short for the usual رؤوسهم, with one wāw doing the work of both the hamza seat and the long ū; it is pointed ruʾusihim in the text and read ruʾūsihim.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا سَائِرِينَ وَالرُّسُلُ تَقْدُمُهُمْ إِلَى أَنْ وَلَّى النَّهَارُ وَأَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ فَنَزَلُوا وَاسْتَرَاحُوا وَبَاتُوا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū sāʾirīna wa-al-rusulu taqdumuhum ilā an wallā al-nahāru wa-aqbala al-laylu fa-nazalū wa-istarāḥū wa-bātū tilka al-layla
sentences.l: And they did not cease being travelling-ones, with the envoys going before them, until the day turned away and the night came on; so they alighted, and rested, and passed that night.
sentences.i: They rode on without halting, the envoys going ahead of them, until the day withdrew and night came on; then they dismounted, rested, and spent that night there.
sentences.n: الرُّسُل here are the envoys of the king of Constantinople who brought the gift in the opening units; they now travel at the head of the army as guides, as the next unit says outright. لَمْ يَزَالُوا is the verb of continuance used with the accusative of a participle (سَائِرِينَ), "they continued travelling". وَلَّى النَّهَارُ is "the day turned its back", the usual way of saying that evening came.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ اللَّهُ بِالصَّبَاحِ رَكِبُوا وَسَارُوا وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا مُجِدِّينَ فِى السَّيْرِ وَالرُّسُلُ يَدُلُّونَهُمْ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ مُدَّةَ عِشْرِينَ يَوْمًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa Allāhu bi-al-ṣabāḥi rakibū wa-sārū wa-lam yazālū mujiddīna fī al-sayri wa-al-rusulu yadullūnahum ʿalā al-ṭarīqi muddata ʿishrīna yawman
sentences.l: And when God brought-on-the-morning with the dawn, they rode and journeyed, and did not cease being earnest-ones in the journeying, the envoys guiding them to the road, a span of twenty days.
sentences.i: And when God brought on the morning with its light, they mounted and travelled on, pressing steadily forward with the envoys showing them the way, for a space of twenty days.
sentences.n: أَصْبَحَ اللَّهُ بِالصَّبَاحِ, literally "God made-the-morning with the morning", is an idiom for the coming of dawn; read it as "day broke". The envoys now guide the army, يَدُلُّونَهُمْ عَلَى الطَّرِيقِ, "they point them to the road". مُدَّةَ is an accusative of duration, "for a span of".

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَشْرَفُوا فِى الْيَوْمِ الْحَادِي وَالْعِشْرِينَ عَلَى وَادٍ وَاسِعِ الْجِهَاتِ كَثِيرِ الْأَشْجَارِ وَالنَّبَاتِ فَسِيحِ النَّوَاحِي
sentences.tr: thumma ashrafū fī al-yawmi al-ḥādī wa-al-ʿishrīna ʿalā wādin wāsiʿi al-jihāti kathīri al-ashjāri wa-al-nabāti fasīḥi al-nawāḥī
sentences.l: Then they overlooked, on the day the-one-and-the-twenty, a valley wide-of the-sides, many-of the-trees and-the-plants, spacious-of the-regions.
sentences.i: Then on the twenty-first day they came out upon a valley, broad on every side, thick with trees and plants, and spacious in its reaches.
sentences.n: أَشْرَفَ عَلَى is 'to come to a height from which one overlooks', so here: 'they came out upon' the valley. The edition prints فى for في; kept as printed. The three adjectives each stand in construct with the part they describe ('wide of sides', 'many of trees'), and all agree in the genitive with وَادٍ.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ وُصُولُهُمْ إِلَى ذَٰلِكَ الْوَادِي لَيْلًا فَأَمَرَهُمْ شَرْكَانُ بِالنُّزُولِ وَالْإِقَامَةِ فِيهِ ثَلَٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna wuṣūluhum ilā dhālika al-wādī laylan fa-amarahum Sharkānu bi-al-nuzūli wa-al-iqāmati fīhi thalāthata ayyāmin
sentences.l: And their arrival at that valley was by night, so Sharkān ordered them to the descending and the staying in it three days.
sentences.i: They reached that valley by night, and Sharkān bade them halt and encamp there for three days.
sentences.n: ثلثة is the edition's spelling of ثلاثة (the long ā is not written); it is pointed with a dagger alif so that it reads thalāthata. أَمَرَ بِـ is the verb's own preposition: 'command (someone) to do, order for'. شَرْكَان (Sharkān) is the hero of this tale, Prince Sharkān, son of King ʿUmar; being a proper name ending in -ān it is diptote and takes no tanwīn.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ الْعَسَاكِرُ وَضَرَبُوا الْخِيَامَ وَافْتَرَقَ الْعَسْكَرُ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا وَنَزَلَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ وَصُحْبَتَهُ رُسُلُ أَفْرِيدُونَ صَاحِبِ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ فِي وَسَطِ ذَٰلِكَ الْوَادِي
sentences.tr: fa-nazala al-ʿasākiru wa-ḍarabū al-khiyāma wa-iftaraqa al-ʿaskaru yamīnan wa-shimālan wa-nazala al-wazīru Dandānu wa-ṣuḥbatahu rusulu Afrīdūna ṣāḥibi al-Qusṭanṭīniyyati fī wasaṭi dhālika al-wādī
sentences.l: So the armies descended, and struck the tents, and the army dispersed right and left; and the vizier Dandān descended, and in his company the messengers of Afrīdūn, lord-of Constantinople, in the middle of that valley.
sentences.i: So the troops dismounted and pitched their tents, and the host spread out to right and left; and the vizier Dandān made camp in the middle of the valley, with the envoys of Afrīdūn, lord of Constantinople, in his company.
sentences.n: فَنَزَلَ الْعَسَاكِرُ puts the verb in the singular before its plural subject, the ordinary Arabic agreement when the verb comes first. ضَرَبَ الْخِيَامَ, 'strike the tents', is the idiom for pitching camp. وَصُحْبَتَهُ is read here as an adverbial accusative, 'and in his company', with the envoys as the nominative that follows; the print gives only the bare letters, so the pointing is ours. Dandān is the old vizier; Afrīdūn is the Byzantine king whose envoys travel with the army.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْمَلِكُ شَرْكَانُ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ فِي وَقْتِ وُصُولِ الْعَسْكَرِ وَقَفَ بَعْدَهُمْ سَاعَةً حَتَّى نَزَلُوا جَمِيعُهُمْ وَتَفَرَّقُوا فِي جَوَانِبِ الْوَادِي فَأَرْخَى عِنَانَ جَوَادِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-maliku Sharkānu fa-innahu kāna fī waqti wuṣūli al-ʿaskari waqafa baʿdahum sāʿatan ḥattā nazalū jamīʿuhum wa-tafarraqū fī jawānibi al-wādī fa-arkhā ʿināna jawādihi
sentences.l: And as for King Sharkān, indeed he, at the time of the army's arrival, had stopped behind them an hour until they had all descended and dispersed in the sides of the valley; and he slackened the rein of his steed.
sentences.i: As for King Sharkān, when the army arrived he had held back behind them for an hour, until they had all dismounted and scattered through the flanks of the valley; and then he let his horse's rein go slack.
sentences.n: كَانَ … وَقَفَ, 'he was / he had stopped', joins كان to a perfect verb to give a pluperfect, a common narrative turn. جَمِيعُهُمْ is a nominative that sums up the subject ('they, all of them'). أَرْخَى عِنَانَ is the idiom for giving a horse its head.

sentences.t: وَأَرَادَأَنْ يَكْشِفَ ذَٰلِكَ الْوَادِيَ وَيَتَوَلَّى الْحَرَسَ بِنَفْسِهِ لِأَحْلِ وَصِيَّةِ وَالِدِهِ لَهُ فَإِنَّهُمْ فِي أَوَّلِ بِلَادِ الرُّومِ وَأَرْضِ الْعِدَ
sentences.tr: wa-arāda an yakshifa dhālika al-wādiya wa-yatawallā al-ḥarasa bi-nafsihi li-aḥli waṣiyyati wālidihi lahu fa-innahum fī awwali bilādi al-Rūmi wa-arḍi al-ʿida
sentences.l: And he wanted that he scout that valley and take-on the guard himself, for the sake of his father's charge to him, for they were in the first of the lands of the Rūm and the land of the enemy.
sentences.i: He meant to scout out that valley and to keep the watch in person, as his father had charged him, for they stood at the very edge of the Byzantine lands, the country of the foe.
sentences.n: Three oddities in a single line. وارادان is printed as one word, أراد أن, 'he wanted that'; we point it أَرَادَأَنْ. لاحل is printed with ح where the sense requires لأجل, 'for the sake of' (ج and ح differ by one dot); the letters are kept and pointed as printed, to be read li-ajli. العد is cut short, almost certainly for العدو or العدا, 'the enemy'; we point what is printed, الْعِدَ, and read it as 'the enemy', which is our guess. الروم are the Rūm, the Byzantines. تَوَلَّى الْحَرَسَ is 'to take charge of the guard'.

sentences.t: وَفَسَارَ وَحْدَهُ بَعْدَأَنْ أَمَرَ مَمَالِيكَهُ وَخَوَاصَّهُ بِالنُّزُولِ عِنْدَ الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-fa-sāra waḥdahu baʿda an amara mamālīkahu wa-khawāṣṣahu bi-al-nuzūli ʿinda al-wazīri Dandāna
sentences.l: And so he set out by himself, after he had ordered his mamluks and his intimates to the descending with the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: And so he rode off alone, having first told his mamluks and his closest men to make camp beside the vizier Dandān.
sentences.n: The edition stacks two conjunctions in وفسار, 'and so'; the و is most likely the missing last letter of العد at the end of the previous unit, which would then read العدو, "the enemy". بعدان is printed as one word, بعد أن, 'after that'; we point it بَعْدَأَنْ. وحده 'by himself' is the stock accusative of state. The mamālīk are his slave-soldiers, and the khawāṣṣ his personal intimates.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ سَارَ عَلَى ظَهْرِ جَوَادِهِ فِي جَانِبِ الْوَادِي إِلَى أَنْ مَضَى مِنَ اللَّيْلِ رُبْعُهُ فَتَعِبَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu sāra ʿalā ẓahri jawādihi fī jānibi al-wādī ilā an maḍā mina al-layli rubʿuhu fa-taʿiba
sentences.l: Then, indeed, he travelled on the back of his steed in a side of the valley until a quarter of the night had passed from it; and he grew tired.
sentences.i: Then he rode along one side of the valley until a quarter of the night was gone, and he grew weary.
sentences.n: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ is a narrative connective, little more than 'then'. مَضَى مِنَ اللَّيْلِ رُبْعُهُ 'a quarter of the night passed' has the part of the night as grammatical subject (رُبْعُهُ) and مِنَ اللَّيْلِ as its 'out of'.

sentences.t: وَغَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ النَّوْمُ فَصَارَ لَايَقْدِرُ أَنْ يَرْكُضَ الْجَوَادَ وَكَانَ لَهُ عَادَةٌ أَنَّهُ يَنَامُ عَلَى ظَهْرِ جَوَادِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ghalaba ʿalayhi al-nawmu fa-ṣāra lāyaqdiru an yarkuḍa al-jawāda wa-kāna lahu ʿādatun annahu yanāmu ʿalā ẓahri jawādihi
sentences.l: And sleep overcame him, so he became not-able that he spur the steed; and there was to him a habit that he sleeps on the back of his steed.
sentences.i: Sleep overcame him, so that he could no longer spur his horse on; and it was a habit of his that he would sleep on his horse's back.
sentences.n: لايقدر is printed as one word, lā yaqdiru, 'he cannot'; kept as printed. صَارَ + imperfect, 'he came to be doing', marks the change of state. عَادَةٌ أَنَّهُ يَنَامُ is 'a habit: that he sleeps', a clause in apposition to the noun.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا هَجَمَ عَلَيْهِ النَّوْمُ نَامَ فَمَا زَالَ الْجَوَادُ سَائِرًا بِهِ إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ فَدَخَلَ بِهِ فِي بَعْضِ الْغَابَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā hajama ʿalayhi al-nawmu nāma fa-mā zāla al-jawādu sāʾiran bihi ilā niṣfi al-layli fa-dakhala bihi fī baʿḍi al-ghābāti
sentences.l: And when sleep rushed upon him, he slept; and the steed did not cease going with him until the middle of the night, and entered with him into some of the thickets.
sentences.i: When sleep fell upon him he slept, and the horse went on carrying him until midnight, and bore him into one of the thickets.
sentences.n: هَجَمَ عَلَيْهِ النَّوْمُ, 'sleep burst in upon him', pictures sleep as an attacker. مَا زَالَ + accusative participle is 'went on being', here سَائِرًا بِهِ 'going with him'. دَخَلَ بِهِ is 'he entered with him', i.e. the horse carried him in; the بِـ makes the intransitive verb take a companion.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تِلْكَ الْغَابَةُ كَثِيرَةَ الْأَشْجَارِ فَلَمْ يَنْتَبِهْ شَرْكَانُ حَتَّى دَقَّ الْجَوَادُ بِحَافِرِهِ فِى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tilka al-ghābatu kathīrata al-ashjāri fa-lam yantabih Sharkānu ḥattā daqqa al-jawādu bi-ḥāfirihi fī al-arḍi
sentences.l: And that thicket was many-of trees, and Sharkān did not wake until the steed pounded with its hoof on the ground.
sentences.i: The thicket was dense with trees, and Sharkān did not stir until the horse stamped its hoof upon the ground.
sentences.n: ينتبه here means 'to become aware, to wake up', not 'to pay attention'. دَقَّ بِحَافِرِهِ is 'to pound with the hoof'; it is the horse's stamp that wakes him.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَيْقَظَ فَوَجَدَ نَفْسَهُ بَيْنَ الْأَشْجَارِ فَطَلَعَ عَلَيْهِ الْقَمَرُ وَأَضَاءَ فِى الْخَافِقَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-istayqaẓa fa-wajada nafsahu bayna al-ashjāri fa-ṭalaʿa ʿalayhi al-qamaru wa-aḍāʾa fī al-khāfiqayni
sentences.l: So he awoke and found himself among the trees, and the moon rose upon him and shone in the two horizons.
sentences.i: He woke and found himself among the trees; then the moon rose over him and lit up the whole sky from edge to edge.
sentences.n: وَجَدَ نَفْسَهُ is the idiom for 'he found himself' (so-and-so). الخافقين, the dual of خافق, are the two quarters where the sky 'flutters' down to the earth, i.e. east and west, so 'the two horizons' means 'everywhere under the sky'. أضاء is intransitive here: the moon 'gave light'.

sentences.t: فَانْدَهَشَ شَرْكَانُ لَمَّا رَأَى نَفْسَهُ فِي ذَٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَقَالَ كَلِمَةً لَايَخْجَلُ قَائِلُهَا وَهِيَ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: fa-andahasha Sharkānu lammā raʾā nafsahu fī dhālika al-makāni wa-qāla kalimatan lāyakhjalu qāʾiluhā wa-hiya lāḥawla wa-lāquwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīm
sentences.l: So Sharkān was bewildered when he saw himself in that place, and said a word whose sayer is not ashamed, and it was: No might and no power except in God, the High, the Great.
sentences.i: Sharkān was bewildered when he saw where he was, and he spoke a word that no one need be ashamed to say: 'There is no might and no power save in God, the High, the Great.'
sentences.n: لاحول ولاقوة (lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata) is printed with each لا joined to the next word; kept as printed. It is the believer's formula of helplessness and trust, spoken on meeting something startling or fearful. لايخجل is likewise printed as one word: lā yakhjalu, 'is not ashamed'. رأى nafsahu 'saw himself' = 'found himself'; the rhyme falls on the closing pair al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīm.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذَٰلِكَ وَهُوَ خَائِفٌ مِنَ الْوَحْشِ وَإِذَا بِالْقَمَرِ قَدِ انْبَسَطَ عَلَى مَرْجٍ كَآنَّهُ مِنْ مُرُوجِ الْجَنَّةِ فَسَمِعَ كَلَامًا مَلِيحًا وَحِسًّا عَالِيًا وَضَحِكًا يَسْبِي عُقُولَ الرِّجَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa kadhālika wa-huwa khāʾifun mina al-waḥshi wa-idhā bi-al-qamari qadi inbasaṭa ʿalā marjin kaʾannahu min murūji al-janna fa-samiʿa kalāman malīḥan wa-ḥissan ʿāliyan wa-ḍaḥikan yasbī ʿuqūla al-rijāl
sentences.l: So while he was thus, and he was afraid of the wild beasts, behold, the moon had spread over a meadow as though it were of the meadows of Paradise; and he heard pleasing speech, and a loud sound, and laughter that captures the minds of men.
sentences.i: And while he stood so, afraid of wild beasts, lo, the moon lay spread over a meadow like one of the meadows of Paradise; and he heard sweet talk and a loud noise, and laughter that would carry off the wits of men.
sentences.n: The sentence is built on بينما … وإذا بـ … فـ: 'while he was so … and behold, … then he heard'. إذا بـ introduces what suddenly appears. The edition prints كآنه with an alif madda in place of كأنه ('as though'); kept as printed, read ka-anna-hu. The moon 'spreads' (انبسط) in the sense that its light lies across the meadow. يَسْبِي عُقُولَ الرِّجَالِ, 'captivates the minds of men', is a stock praise of women's laughter.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ الْمَلِكُ شَرْكَانُ عَنْ جَوَادِهِ وَرَبَطَهُ فِى الْأَشْجَارِ وَمَشَى حَتَّى أَشْرَفَ عَلَى نَهْرِ مَاءٍ يَجْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-nazala al-maliku Sharkānu ʿan jawādihi wa-rabaṭahu fī al-ashjāri wa-mashā ḥattā ashrafa ʿalā nahri māʾin yajrī
sentences.l: So King Sharkān descended from his steed, and tied it among the trees, and walked until he overlooked a river of water that flows.
sentences.i: King Sharkān dismounted, tied his horse among the trees, and walked on until he came out above a running stream.
sentences.n: نَزَلَ عَنْ takes ʿan for what one gets down from. The edition prints فى and يجري with their usual spellings; kept. نَهْرُ مَاءٍ يَجْرِي, 'a river of flowing water', is a stock phrase for a clear running stream.

sentences.t: وَسَمِعَ كَلَامَ امْرَأَةٍ تَتَكَلَّمُ بِالْعَرَبِيِّ وَهِيَ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-samiʿa kalāma imraʾatin tatakallamu bi-al-ʿarabiyyi wa-hiya taqūlu
sentences.l: And he heard the speech of a woman speaking in Arabic, and she was saying:
sentences.i: He heard the voice of a woman speaking Arabic, and this is what she said:
sentences.n: تَتَكَلَّمُ بِالْعَرَبِيِّ, 'speaks in the Arabic', uses بِـ to name the language spoken; the sentence ends with the introduction to her words, which follow.

sentences.t: وَحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ لَيْسَ هَٰذَا مِنْكُنَّ مَلِيحٌ وَلَٰكِنْ كُلُّ مَنْ تَكَلَّمَتْ بِكَلِمَةٍ صَرَعْتُهَا وَكَتَفْتُهَا بِزُنَّارِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi laysa hādhā minkunna malīḥun wa-lākin kullu man takallamat bi-kalimatin ṣaraʿtuhā wa-kataftuhā bi-zunnārihā
sentences.l: By the right of the Messiah, this is not nice from you; but every one who has spoken a word, I throw her down and bind her with her girdle.
sentences.i: By the Messiah's truth, this is not well done of you; whichever of you speaks a word, I will fling her down and tie her up with her own girdle.
sentences.n: وحق المسيح is an oath, 'by the right of the Messiah', in the mouth of a Christian (Byzantine) woman; she is the voice Sharkān has just heard speaking Arabic, and the threat is addressed to her companions. ليس هذا منكن مليح has the predicate مليح in the nominative; Classical would put it in the accusative after ليس, so this is the loose Middle Arabic order, and we point what is printed. The two perfects صرعتها وكتفتها are first person: 'I fling her down and bind her' (a threat stated as a fact). الزنار is the girdle, in particular the belt worn by non-Muslim subjects and Christians.

sentences.t: كُلُّ هَٰذَا وَشَرْكَانُ يَمْشِي إِلَى جِهَةِ الصَّوْتِ حَتَّى انْتَهَى إِلَى طَرَفِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: kullu hādhā wa-Sharkānu yamshī ilā jihati al-ṣawti ḥattā intahā ilā ṭarafi al-makāni
sentences.l: All this, and Sharkān walking toward the direction of the voice, until he reached the edge of the place.
sentences.i: All this while Sharkān was walking toward the sound of the voice, until he came to the edge of the place.
sentences.n: كُلُّ هَٰذَا is a loose opening, 'all this (went on)', with وَشَرْكَانُ يَمْشِي as a circumstantial clause; read it as 'all this while'.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ فَإِذَا هُوَ بِنَهْرٍ يَسْبَحُ وَطَيْرٍ تَمْرَحُ وَغِزْلَانٍ تَسْرَحُ وَوُحُوشٍ تَرْتَعُ وَالطُّيُورُ بِاخْتِلَافِ لُغَاتِهَا لِمَعَانِى الْحَظِّ تَشْرَحُ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara fa-idhā huwa bi-nahrin yasbaḥu wa-ṭayrin tamraḥu wa-ghizlānin tasraḥu wa-wuḥūshin tartaʿu wa-al-ṭuyūru bi-ikhtilāfi lughātihā li-maʿānī al-ḥaẓẓi tashraḥu
sentences.l: So he looked, and behold, he was at a river flowing, and birds frolicking, and gazelles roaming, and wild beasts grazing, and the birds, by the difference of their tongues, explaining the meanings of good fortune.
sentences.i: He looked, and there was a river streaming, birds frolicking, gazelles roaming and wild beasts grazing, while the birds, each in its own tongue, sang out the meanings of good fortune.
sentences.n: فَإِذَا هُوَ بِـ 'and behold, he was at / there was' — the بِـ after إذا of surprise only marks what appears, and the four things seen all stand in the genitive after it: نَهْرٍ, طَيْرٍ, غِزْلَانٍ, وُحُوشٍ. The four present verbs يَسْبَحُ تَمْرَحُ تَسْرَحُ تَرْتَعُ then تَشْرَحُ, all on -aḥu/-aʿu, make a run of sajʿ. طَيْر is a collective, hence feminine verb تَمْرَحُ. The edition prints لمعانى with ى; kept.

sentences.t: وَذَٰلِكَ الْمَكَانُ مُزَرْكَشٌ بِأَنْوَاعِ النَّبَاتِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ بَعْضُ وَاصِفِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-dhālika al-makānu muzarkashun bi-anwāʿi al-nabāti kamā qāla fīhi baʿḍu wāṣifīhi
sentences.l: And that place was embroidered with kinds of plants, as one of its describers said of it
sentences.i: That place was embroidered all over with every kind of plant, as one of those who have described it said of it:
sentences.n: مُزَرْكَشٌ is 'embroidered, brocaded', from the Persian zarkash 'gold-working'; used of a landscape it means 'flowered over'. The sentence runs on into the next unit, where the two verses are introduced.

sentences.t: هَٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْ—تَيْنِ
sentences.tr: hādhayni al-bayti—tayni
sentences.l: these two verses
sentences.i: these two verses
sentences.n: The edition prints a long dash in the middle of البيتين; we keep it as printed. The two verses follow.

sentences.t:
مَا تَحْسُنُ الْاَرْضُ اِلَّا عِنْدَ زَهْرَتِهَا * وَالْمَاءُ مِنْ فَوْقِهَا يَجْرِي بِاِرْسَالِ
صُنْعُ الْاِلَهِ الْعَظِيمِ الشَّانِ مُقْتَدِرًا * مُعْطِى الْعَطَايَا وَمُعْطِي كُلِّ اِفْضَالِ
sentences.tr:
mā taḥsunu al-arḍu illā ʿinda zahratihā * wa-al-māʾu min fawqihā yajrī bi-irsāli
ṣunʿu al-ilāhi al-ʿaẓīmi al-shāni muqtadiran * muʿṭī al-ʿaṭāyā wa-muʿṭī kulli afḍāli
sentences.l:
The earth is not beautiful save at its blossoming * and the water, from above it, runs with a letting-loose.
The making of the God, great-of the-station, [being] all-powerful * giver-of the gifts and giver-of every bestowal.
sentences.i: The earth is never lovelier than in its flowering, while the water above it runs in a free-flowing stream: the handiwork of the mighty God, all-powerful, giver of gifts and giver of every bounty.
sentences.n: The verse is copied exactly as the edition prints it, vowel marks and all. The first line is about the garden the prince is looking at; the second turns to praise of the Maker. مُقْتَدِرًا is an accusative of circumstance describing God, and مُعْطِى is spelled with a final alif maqṣūra (ى), though it is the same participle as the مُعْطِي in the other half-line, 'giver'. Note too the printed اِفْضَالِ with a bare alif and a kasra, which we read as the plain noun إفضال 'bestowal of favour'.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ شَرْكَانُ إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ فَرَأَى فِيهِ دَيْرًا وَمِنْ دَاخِلِ الدَّيْرِ قَلْعَةٌ شَاهِقَةٌ فِى الْهَوَاءِ فِي ضَوْءِ الْقَمَرِ وَفِي وَسَطِهَا نَهْرٌ يَجْرِي الْمَاءُ مِنْهُ إِلَى تِلْكَ الرِّيَاضِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara Sharkāna ilā dhālika al-makāni fa-raʾā fīhi dayran wa-min dākhili al-dayri qalʿatun shāhiqatun fī al-hawāʾi fī ḍawʾi al-qamari wa-fī wasaṭihā nahrun yajrī al-māʾu minhu ilā tilka al-riyāḍ
sentences.l: So Sharkān looked at that place, and saw in it a monastery, and from-inside the monastery a lofty fortress in the air, in the light of the moon, and in the midst of it a river, the water running from it to those gardens.
sentences.i: Sharkān gazed at the place and saw in it a monastery, and within the monastery a fortress towering into the air in the moonlight, with a river in its midst whose water ran out into those gardens.
sentences.n: The edition spells 'in' with ى once (فى الهواء) and with ي elsewhere (فِيهِ, في ضوء, وفي وسطها); every one is read fī and each is kept as printed. وَمِنْ دَاخِلِ الدَّيْرِ قَلْعَةٌ is a clause with no verb: the prepositional phrase 'from inside the monastery' stands first and the subject قَلْعَةٌ follows, so 'there was a fortress'.

sentences.t: وَهُنَاكَ اِمْرَأَةٌ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا عَشْرُ جَوَارٍ كَأَنَّهُنَّ الْأَقْمَارُ وَعَلَيْهِنَّ مِنْ أَنْوَاعِ الْحُلِيِّ وَالْحُلَلِ مَايُدْهِشُ الْأَبْصَارَ وَكُلُّهُنَّ أَبْكَارٌ
sentences.tr: wa-hunāka imraʾatun bayna yadayhā ʿashru jawārin ka-annahunna al-aqmāru wa-ʿalayhinna min anwāʿi al-ḥuliyyi wa-al-ḥulali māyudhishu al-abṣāra wa-kulluhunna abkār
sentences.l: And there, a woman, between her two hands ten slave-girls, as-if-they the moons, and upon them, of kinds-of the-jewellery and the-robes, what bewilders the sights; and all-of-them virgins.
sentences.i: And there was a woman with ten handmaidens before her, like so many moons, and upon them such kinds of jewellery and raiment as dazzle the eyes; and every one of them was a virgin.
sentences.n: بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا, 'between her two hands', means 'in front of her, in her service'. عَشْرُ جَوَارٍ puts the counted noun in the genitive plural, as numbers from three to ten require; جَوَارٍ is a 'defective' plural, the plural of جَارِيَة 'slave-girl'. The edition prints مايدهش as one word, mā + yudhishu, and it is kept glued: 'what bewilders'. The print has precomposed hamza in كأنهن, kept exactly as printed. أَبْكَار is the plural of بِكْر 'virgin'.

sentences.t: كَمَا قِيلَ فِيهِنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ
sentences.tr: ka-mā qīla fīhinna hādhihi al-abyātu
sentences.l: As was said concerning them, these verses.
sentences.i: As these verses say of them:
sentences.n: This is the usual lead-in to a poem. The passive قِيلَ takes the verses as its (nominative) stand-in subject, 'these verses were said of them'. The poem follows in the next unit.

sentences.t:
يُشْرِقُ الْمَرْجُ بِمَافِيهِ * مِنَ الْبِيضِ الْغَوَانِي
زَادَ حُسْنًا وَجَمَالًا * مِنْ بَدِيعَاتِ الْخِلَالِ
كُلُّ عَذْرَاءَ خَلُوبٍ * ذَاتُ غُنْجٍ وَدَلَالِ
رَاخِيَاتٍ لِشُعُورٍ * كَعَنَاقِيدِ اللَّ وَالِي
فَاتِنَاتٍ بِعُيُونٍ * رَامِيَاتٍ بِالنِّبَالِ
مَائِسَاتٍ قَاتِلَاتٍ * لِصَنَادِيدِ الرِّجَالِ
sentences.tr:
yushriqu al-marju bi-māfīhi * mina al-bīḍi al-ghawānī
zāda ḥusnan wa-jamālan * min badīʿāti al-khilāli
kullu ʿadhrāʾa khalūbin * dhātu ghunjin wa-dalāli
rākhiyātin li-shuʿūrin * ka-ʿanāqīdi al-l wālī
fātinātin bi-ʿuyūnin * rāmiyātin bi-al-nibāli
māʾisātin qātilātin * li-ṣanādīdi al-rijāli
sentences.l:
The meadow shines with what is in it * of the white [women], the fair ones.
It increased in beauty and comeliness * through wondrous [ones] of traits.
Every virgin, ravishing * possessed-of coquetry and wantonness,
letting-down, for tresses * like bunches of the l-wālī,
bewitching with eyes * shooting with arrows,
swaying, slaying * to the chieftains of men.
sentences.i: The meadow glows with all that is in it, with fair white-skinned beauties; its loveliness and charm grew greater still through their marvellous graces. Each is a ravishing maiden, full of coquetry and playful pride, letting down tresses like clusters on the vine, bewitching with their eyes, shooting arrows from them, swaying as they walk, slaying the champions among men.
sentences.n: The printed text breaks a word in line four, كَعَنَاقِيدِ اللَّ وَالِي, with a space between اللَّ and وَالِي; the whole phrase is kept exactly as printed. The likely word is الدَّوَالِي 'the vines', that is, 'like clusters of the vine', which suits عَنَاقِيد 'bunches'; but the edition's lām for dāl is a possible misprint and we cannot be sure, so this is only a guess. بِمَافِيهِ is printed glued, bi-mā fīhi. مِنَ الْبِيضِ الْغَوَانِي 'of the white ones, the fair ones' means light-skinned beauties. In line four لِشُعُورٍ is the lām that marks the thing a participle acts on (letting down for/of tresses), a poetic choice instead of the plain accusative.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ شَرْكَانُ إِلَى هَؤُلَاءِ الْعَشَرَةِ جَوَارٍ فَوَجَدَ بَيْنَهُنَّ جَارِيَةً كَأَنَّهَا الْبَدْرُ عِنْدَ تَمَامِهِ بِشَعْرٍ أَجْعَدَوَ جَبِينٍ أَبْلَجَ وَطَرْفٍ أَدْعَجَ وَصُدْغٍ مُعَقْرَبٍ كَامِلَةً فِى الذَّاتِ وَالصِّفَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara Sharkānu ilā hāʾulāʾi al-ʿashirati jawārin fa-wajada baynahunna jāriyatan ka-annahā al-badru ʿinda tamāmihi bi-shaʿrin ajʿada wa-jabīnin ablaja wa-ṭarfin adʿaja wa-ṣudghin muʿaqrabin kāmilatan fī al-dhāti wa-al-ṣifāt
sentences.l: So Sharkān looked at these ten slave-girls and found among them a girl as-if-she the full moon at its fullness, with hair curly, and a forehead bright, and an eye black-and-large-eyed, and a temple-lock scorpion-curled, perfect in the essence and the qualities.
sentences.i: Then Sharkān looked at these ten handmaidens and found among them one like the full moon at its fullest, with curling hair and a shining brow, with great dark eyes and scorpion-curled locks at her temples, flawless in her person and in her qualities.
sentences.n: Two points of spelling. First, اجعدو is printed as one word, but it is أَجْعَد 'curly' followed by the conjunction و 'and', run together by the printer; it is vocalized as أَجْعَدَوَ, read ajʿada wa-, and the following word جَبِينٍ is then another noun in the chain: 'with hair curly, and a forehead bright'. Second, هَؤُلَاءِ and كَأَنَّهَا keep the precomposed hamza the edition prints. الْعَشَرَةِ جَوَارٍ puts a definite numeral before an indefinite plural, loose Middle Arabic (Classical would say الْجَوَارِيَ الْعَشْرَ). مُعَقْرَب is 'scorpion-like', a temple-lock curled up like a scorpion's tail, an old image of beauty. أَدْعَج means black-eyed with large eyes; أَبْلَج is a bright, unfurrowed brow. كَامِلَةً is an accusative of circumstance describing the girl.

sentences.t: كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرًا
sentences.tr: ka-mā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿran
sentences.l: As said concerning her the poet these verses, in verse.
sentences.i: As the poet has said of her, in these verses:
sentences.n: The printed line break falls inside this sentence (before الأبيات) and has been dropped. The edition's شعرا (accusative, 'as poetry') is redundant after الْأَبْيَاتَ, a padding that lead-ins to poems often show. Here الْأَبْيَاتَ is accusative as the object of قَالَ, unlike the passive قِيلَ in the earlier lead-in.

sentences.t:
تَزْهُو عَلَيَّ بِالْحَاظِ بَدِيعَاتِ * وَقَدُّهَا مُخْجِلُ لِلسَّمْهَرِيَّاتِ
تَبْدُو اِلَيْنَا وَخَدَّاهَا مُوَرَّدَةٌ * فِيهَا مِنَ الظَّرْفِ اَنْوَاعُ الْمَلَاحَاتِ
كَأَنَّ طُرَّتَهَا مِنْ فَوْقِ طَلْعَتِهَا * لَيْلٌ يَلُوحُ عَلَى صُبْحِ الْمَسَرَّاتِ
sentences.tr:
tazhū ʿalayya bi-alḥāẓi badīʿāti * wa-qadduhā mukhjilu li-al-samhariyyāti
tabdū ilaynā wa-khaddāhā muwarradatun * fīhā mina al-ẓarfi anwāʿu al-malāḥāti
ka-anna ṭurratahā min fawqi ṭalʿatihā * laylun yalūḥu ʿalā ṣubḥi al-masarrāti
sentences.l:
She is-haughty over me with glances, wondrous ones, * and her stature is shaming to the lances.
She appears to us, her two cheeks rose-coloured, * in her, of elegance, kinds of prettiness.
As-if her forelock above her countenance * [were] a night gleaming over the morning of the delights.
sentences.i: She carries herself proudly before me with marvellous glances, and her figure puts the lances to shame; she comes into view, her cheeks rose-red, with every kind of grace and charm in her. Her forelock, above her radiant face, is a night glimmering upon the dawn of delights.
sentences.n: The verse is copied as printed. بِالْحَاظِ is printed with a bare alif and could look like the article الـ after بِ, but it is the plural أَلْحَاظ 'glances' (bi-alḥāẓ, 'with glances'). مُخْجِلُ is printed without tanwīn, as the edition has it. السَّمْهَرِيَّات are the lances of Samhar, the famous maker of spears, so the poet likens her slender stature to a lance and says she shames it. الْمَسَرَّات is the plural of مَسَرَّة 'delight'.

sentences.t: فَسَمِعَهَا شَرْكَانُ وَهِيَ تَقُولُ لِلْجَوَارِي تَقَدَّمُوا حَتَّى أُصَارِعَكُمْ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَغِيبَ الْقَمَرُ وَيَأْتِىَ الصَّبَاحُ
sentences.tr: fa-samiʿahā Sharkānu wa-hiya taqūlu li-al-jawārī taqaddamū ḥattā uṣāriʿakum qabla an yaghība al-qamaru wa-yaʾtiya al-ṣabāḥ
sentences.l: So Sharkān heard her, she saying to the slave-girls: 'Advance, so that I wrestle you, before the moon sets and the morning comes.'
sentences.i: Sharkān heard her saying to the girls, 'Come forward, and I will wrestle every one of you before the moon goes down and the morning comes.'
sentences.n: The 'her' is the fair girl just described. The edition prints a final ى instead of ي in يأتى, and it is pointed as printed; it also prints the precomposed hamza there, which is kept. حَتَّى with the subjunctive أُصَارِعَكُمْ is purposive, 'so that I may wrestle you', not 'until'; ṣāraʿa (form III) takes its opponent as a direct object.

sentences.t: فَصَارَتْ كُلُّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُنَّ تَتَقَدَّمُ إِلَيْهَا فَتَصْرَعُهَا فِى الْحَالِ وَتَكْتِفُهَا بِزُنَّارِهَا فَلَمْ تَزَلْ تُصَارِعُهُنَّ وَتَصْرَعُهُنَّ حَتَّى صَرَعَتِ الْجَمِيعَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣārat kullu wāḥidatin minhunna tataqaddamu ilayhā fa-taṣraʿuhā fī al-ḥāli wa-taktifuhā bi-zunnārihā fa-lam tazal tuṣāriʿuhunna wa-taṣraʿuhunna ḥattā ṣaraʿati al-jamīʿa
sentences.l: So each one of them became advancing toward her, and she threw her down at once and bound her arms with her girdle; and she did not cease wrestling them and throwing them, until she had thrown them all.
sentences.i: One after another the girls came forward to meet her, and each in turn she threw at once and trussed up with her own girdle; and so she went on wrestling them and throwing them until she had laid them all low.
sentences.n: صَارَتْ + imperfect is 'began to' (the inchoative use of ṣāra); the singular كُلُّ وَاحِدَةٍ is why the pronouns that follow are singular, 'she threw her'. The zunnār is the girdle that Christians wore, and it marks the girls as Christians, which fits the oaths by the Messiah in this exchange. لَمْ تَزَلْ + imperfect is the familiar 'she did not cease', i.e. 'she went on'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَتْ إِلَى الْجَارِيَةِ عَجُوزٍ كَانَتْ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma iltafatat ilā al-jāriyati ʿajūzin kānat bayna yadayhā
sentences.l: Then she turned to the slave-girl, an old woman, who was between her two hands.
sentences.i: Then she turned to an old serving-woman who stood before her.
sentences.n: The edition prints the definite الجارية before the indefinite عجوز, where one would expect جارية عجوز, 'an old female slave'. The pair is read as apposition, 'the slave-woman, an old woman', and point عَجُوزٍ as genitive; the print is kept as it stands. بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا, 'between her two hands', is the ordinary 'in front of her, at her side'.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهَا الْعَجُوزُ وَهِيَ كَالْمُغْضَبَةِ عَلَيْهَا يَا فَاجِرَةُ أَتَفْرَحِينَ بِصَرْعِكِ لِلْجَوَارِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahā al-ʿajūzu wa-hiya ka-al-mughḍabati ʿalayhā yā fājiratu a-tafraḥīna bi-ṣarʿiki li-al-jawārī
sentences.l: And the old woman said to her, she being like the one-made-angry at her: 'O wanton one! Do you rejoice in your throwing-down of the slave-girls?'
sentences.i: And the old woman, looking like one put out with her, said, 'You wanton strumpet! Are you proud of having thrown those girls?'
sentences.n: كَالْمُغْضَبَةِ is 'like one who has been angered' (a passive participle of form IV); the old woman puts on the manner of anger, and the text leaves open how much of it is real. فَاجِرَة is a woman of dissolute, unchaste ways, a coarse insult; with يَا it takes the damma of a vocative. The initial أَ of أَتَفْرَحِينَ is the question particle, and فَرِحَ بِـ is 'rejoice in, be pleased with'.

sentences.t: فَهَا أَنَا عَجُوزٌ وَقَدْ أَصْرَعْتُهُنَّ أَرْبَعِينَ مَرَّةً فَكَيْفَ تَعْجَبِينَ بِنَفْسِكِ وَلَكِنْ إِنْ كَانَ لَكِ قُوَّةٌ عَلَى مُصَارَعَتِي فَصَارِعِينِي حَتَّى أَقُومَ إِلَيْكِ وَأَجْعَلَ رَأْسَكِ بَيْنَ رِجْلَيْكِ
sentences.tr: fa-hā anā ʿajūzun wa-qad aṣraʿtuhunna arbaʿīna marratan fa-kayfa taʿjabīna bi-nafsiki wa-lākin in kāna laki quwwatun ʿalā muṣāraʿatī fa-ṣāriʿīnī ḥattā aqūma ilayki wa-ajʿala raʾsaki bayna rijlayki
sentences.l: 'Here am I, an old woman, and I have thrown them forty times; so how can you be vain of yourself? But if there is to you strength for wrestling me, then wrestle me, until I rise to you and put your head between your two legs.'
sentences.i: 'Look at me: an old woman, and I have thrown those girls forty times over! What have you to be vain about? But if you have the strength to wrestle me, then come, wrestle me, and I will get up and put your head between your legs.'
sentences.n: أَصْرَعْتُهُنَّ is a form-IV verb where Classical Arabic would have the form-I صَرَعْتُهُنَّ (which the narrator uses a few units earlier for the same act); it is pointed as printed. عَجِبَ بِنَفْسِهِ is 'to be conceited, vain of oneself'. The 'if' clause with فَـ before its answer is ordinary: إِنْ كَانَ لَكِ قُوَّةٌ … فَصَارِعِينِي. Note that the old woman's threat is a frank bodily one: head between the legs.

sentences.t: فَتَبَسَّمَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ ظَاهِرًا وَقَدِ امْتَلَأَتْ غَيْظًا مِنْهَا بَاطِنًا
sentences.tr: fa-tabassamati al-jāriyatu ẓāhiran wa-qadi imtalaʾat ghayẓan minhā bāṭinan
sentences.l: So the girl smiled outwardly, while she had filled with rage at her inwardly.
sentences.i: The girl smiled on the surface, though within she was brimming with rage at her.
sentences.n: ظَاهِرًا and بَاطِنًا are adverbial accusatives, 'outwardly' and 'inwardly'; مَلَأَ/امْتَلَأَ takes the thing it is full of as an accusative of specification, غَيْظًا, 'full as to rage'. The edition itself prints the precomposed hamza in امتلأت, so it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَقَامَتْ إِلَيْهَا وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَا سِتِّي ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي بِحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ أَتُصَارِعِينَنِي حَقِيقَةً أَمْ تَمْزَحِينَ مَعِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāmat ilayhā wa-qālat lahā yā sittī dhāta al-dawāhī bi-ḥaqqi al-Masīḥi a-tuṣāriʿīnanī ḥaqīqatan am tamzaḥīna maʿī
sentences.l: And she rose to her and said to her: 'O my lady, owner-of the-calamities, by the right of the Messiah, do you wrestle me in truth, or are you joking with me?'
sentences.i: She stood up to face her and said, 'My lady, Lady of Calamities, by the Messiah, do you really mean to wrestle me, or are you jesting?'
sentences.n: The edition prints ستي, read here as sittī, 'my lady' (a short spelling of سيدتي). ذَاتَ الدَّوَاهِي, literally 'she of the calamities', is the old woman's byname, from dāhiya, a dire calamity. بِحَقِّ الْمَسِيحِ, 'by the right of the Messiah', is a Christian oath. In أَتُصَارِعِينَنِي the first أَ is the question particle and the doubled nūn is the verb's -īna plus the nūn of protection before the -ī of 'me'; أَمْ introduces the second half of the either-or question.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ لَهَا نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qālat lahā naʿam
sentences.l: She said to her: 'Yes.'
sentences.i: 'Yes,' the old woman said.
sentences.n: The speaker is the old woman, answering the girl's question in the previous unit.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَ——————بَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, so she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazad, and she fell silent, holding back from the speech she was allowed.
sentences.n: This is the night-closing formula. The edition breaks the last word with a run of dashes; they are kept where they stand and the word is read as الْمُبَاح, 'the permitted', the stock epithet of Shahrazād's storytelling. Note that the grammatical subject is the morning, and Shahrazād is the one overtaken.
